what_its_for: Satralizumab-mwge is used to treat neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD) in adults who have a specific antibody called anti-AQP4 (aquaporin-4). NMOSD is a rare disease that attacks your optic nerves (which affect your vision) and your spinal cord. This medicine helps reduce attacks and flare-ups of this disease.
how_to_take: This medicine is given as an injection just under the skin (subcutaneous injection), usually in your stomach area, thigh, or upper arm. Your doctor or nurse will train you on how to give yourself the injection at home using a prefilled syringe. Always rotate the injection site each time so you do not inject into the exact same spot twice in a row. Do not inject into skin that is red, bruised, tender, or hard.
dosing: The usual dose is 120 mg injected under the skin. You will receive your first three doses at weeks 0, 2, and 4 (called the loading doses). After that, you will receive 120 mg once every 4 weeks (about once a month) as a maintenance dose. Always follow your doctor's exact instructions for your dosing schedule.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, give yourself the injection as soon as you remember. Then continue on your regular schedule. If it is almost time for your next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and just take the next one at the regular time. Do not give yourself two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. Call your doctor or pharmacist if you are unsure what to do.
storage: Store the prefilled syringes in the refrigerator between 36°F and 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Keep them in the original carton to protect them from light. Do not freeze this medication and do not use it if it has been frozen. If needed, you may store the syringe at room temperature (up to 86°F or 30°C) for up to 8 days, but do not put it back in the refrigerator after it has been kept at room temperature. Throw away any syringe that has been at room temperature for more than 8 days. Keep out of reach of children.
what_to_avoid: Avoid receiving live vaccines (such as measles, mumps, rubella, varicella, or nasal flu vaccine) while taking this medication without first talking to your doctor, as this medicine can weaken your immune system. Avoid contact with people who are sick with contagious infections when possible. Tell all of your healthcare providers that you are taking this medicine before any vaccinations or procedures.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor right away if you notice any of the following: signs of a serious infection such as fever, chills, cough, or feeling very unwell; unusual tiredness or weakness; changes in your vision; redness, swelling, warmth, or pain around an injection site that seems to be getting worse; symptoms of liver problems such as yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine, or stomach pain; signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, itching, swelling of the face or throat, or trouble breathing; or any new or worsening symptoms. Also call your doctor before getting any vaccines.
when_it_works: This medicine works over time to help prevent attacks of NMOSD. You may not feel a difference right away. It is important to keep taking it on schedule even if you feel well, because it is working to prevent future flare-ups. Talk to your doctor if you have any concerns about how the medicine is working for you.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Tell your doctor right away if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. It is not yet fully known whether this medicine is safe during pregnancy or if it passes into breast milk. You and your doctor will need to weigh the risks and benefits together. Older adults: This medicine can be used in older adults, but your doctor will monitor you closely for infections and other side effects. Children: Safety and effectiveness in patients under 18 years of age have not been established.
